text:
This tour comes in two parts.
Part one follows a job from start to finish.
Part two shows the tools, your projects and your settings.
Pause it any time.
You can play it again from the Video button at the top of the app.
Every direction in the app is shown two ways: degrees true, for maps and G P S, and the compass reading, with magnetic declination built in, so it works offline.

A real example: a five point eight gigahertz link between two buildings ten miles apart.
The free-space loss is about one hundred thirty-two decibels.
At the middle of the path, sixty percent of the first [Fresnel](/fɹənˈɛl/) zone is about twenty-eight feet, so the line of sight has to clear the trees and roofs by that much.

Radio horizon: a hundred-foot tower talking to a portable radio at five feet reaches about seventeen miles over smooth earth.
A ridge thirty feet above the line, two miles from one end and three from the other, adds about nine and a half decibels of loss at four hundred sixty megahertz.

Coverage, with real numbers.
For a four hundred sixty megahertz repeater on a hundred fifty-foot tower over suburban ground, the Okumura-Hata model gives about one hundred forty-six decibels of loss at eight miles.
With fifty dB m of power out, a portable hears about minus ninety-six dB m there, well above its minus one hundred nineteen sensitivity.

At nineteen hundred megahertz in a city, the COST two thirty-one model gives about one hundred sixty-one decibels at three miles from a hundred-foot site.
Higher frequencies need closer sites.

Predictions are medians.
With an eight decibel spread, a ten decibel margin gives ninety percent coverage at the edge, and about ninety-seven percent of the area.
Drive test the site, and the calibration fits the model to your readings.

L F and H F examples.
At one point seven megahertz with one kilowatt, the ground wave at fifty kilometers is about four millivolts per meter over sea water, but only about point one seven over dry, rocky ground.
The ground decides the range.
For sky wave, the highest usable frequency is about nine megahertz for a five hundred kilometer hop, and about seventeen for fifteen hundred.

That's the end of part one.
Part two, with the tools, your projects and your settings, starts next.

Welcome to part two.
These tools open any time, from Tools and reference near the bottom of the menu.
After them come your projects and your settings.

Floor Plan to [2D](/tˌu dˈi/) and [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/) turns a floor plan or blueprint into a true-scale model.
Drag a P D F, D X F, J P G or P N G file onto the upload box.
Here is a real example: a vector P D F of a one-story office, drawn at one quarter inch equals one foot.

The app reads the scale from the title block, traces the walls, and finds three doors, two windows and four rooms.
The building comes out sixty-four feet six inches by forty feet six inches, about twenty-four hundred square feet.
It grades an A.

Pick a drawing scale, like one quarter inch or one eighth inch to the foot, or type your own.
Choose the sheet size, then print it to scale.
Tick Include in project documentation, and the plan goes into Reports.

The Live view button, at the top of the design pages, shows the [2D](/tˌu dˈi/) plan or the [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/) model in picture in picture, or in its own window.
It stays open while you fill in other pages, and changes as you type.

Project Build Output shows the finished project as it is built: the title block, the sheet index, the floor plans with layers, the [3D](/θɹˌi dˈi/) model, the schedules, and what was added when.
Every missing item links to the page where you add it.

The Calculators page has calculators for cabling, power, fire alarm, sound, radio and antennas.
The [azimuth](/ˈæzəməθ/) calculator takes two G P S positions or addresses, or two project sites.
Results can be applied to the project, and Low-Voltage and R F Design Principles opens the matching calculators.

Site conditions shows the values at the project that change a result: the magnetic field and storms from the Magnetic page, the weather from the Weather page, and U S G S data, such as the iron in the soil.
A cold forecast, for example, raises the battery size.
Remove any of them from a calculation, or add it back.

Low-Voltage and R F Design Principles explains how each system works, and the R F engineering behind it, in plain language.
Under many sections, Calculators opens the matching calculator, and Open takes you to the page that puts it to work.

The R F Spectrum Analyzer turns a U S B receiver into a spectrum analyzer.
Plug in a tiny S A, an R T L S D R or a Hack R F, and press Connect.
The list shows which receivers are plugged in, how far each one tunes, and how accurate its levels are.

With no receiver, tap Use test signals for built-in signals in the eight hundred megahertz band.
The self-test finds the eight fifty-one megahertz carrier within a kilohertz, reads its channel power at about minus sixty-six dB m, and flags the intermod product made by the two carriers.

The Audio and Acoustic Analyzer is a sound level meter and real-time analyzer.
Calibrate with a ninety-four dB calibrator, and readings are in dB S P L, with A, C or Z weighting.

The calibration library has typical curves for measurement mics, phones and tablets.
Search for your mic and tap Use, and the badge shows Mic calibration on.
For the best accuracy, add the file made for your mic's serial number.
It is saved in the app, and works offline.

Measure the room plays a sine sweep through the speakers, and works out the reverberation time by octave and the speech transmission index.
A classroom with about one second of reverberation and a quiet background comes out around zero point five eight, which passes the [NFPA](/ˌɛnˌɛfpˌiˈA/) seventy-two target of zero point five.

The fire alarm audibility test measures the room for sixty seconds, then the alarm.
In public mode, the alarm must be fifteen dB over the average, or five dB over the loudest sound.
Each test saves a signed report under Reports, for the Final Testing records.

Space weather maps show NOAA's aurora forecast and the H F radio blackout map.
Each one downloads again when NOAA makes a new one, and the last copy is kept for offline use.

The declination map shows lines of equal compass declination across the country for today, from the high-resolution magnetic model built into the app.
It works with no internet.

The radar map is NOAA's live radar, refreshed every five minutes, with alert areas outlined.
Tap Play last hour to loop the past hour, and see where the storms are heading.
